title: Adverse media screening: how to review a hit
summary: Many adverse media hits are about someone else, and many of the rest need context. How to resolve a hit, read what it alleges, and record the decision.
body_markdown:
The search of news and other public sources for negative information about a customer or the people who own and control it, particularly anything that points to financial crime such as fraud, corruption, money laundering or sanctions evasion. It is also called negative news screening, and it usually sits alongside sanctions and politically exposed person screening in customer due diligence.


Reporting that connects a person or business to financial crime or to conduct that creates similar risk: fraud, bribery and corruption, money laundering, tax crime, sanctions evasion and organised crime, among others. Negative coverage that has nothing to do with those risks, such as a bad product review, is usually out of scope.


Sanctions screening compares names against official lists, so a confirmed match points to a defined entry. Adverse media screening searches news articles and other free text, so each hit has to be resolved to the right person and then read to see what it alleges and how far the matter went. That makes it noisier and slower to review.


Match on more than the name. Compare secondary identifiers such as date of birth, location, occupation and the other people named. Clear a hit when a strong identifier such as a date of birth clearly differs, and treat location or occupation as supporting evidence only. Group repeated coverage of the same story, and record the reason for every cleared hit, so the decision can be checked later and the same article does not have to be reviewed again.


There is no single answer. Firms set a look-back period to suit their risk appetite, and industry guidance suggests a multi-year period may be appropriate, with longer or shorter periods for different kinds of offence. An older story still counts, and it should be read alongside what happened afterwards, such as a dismissal or an acquittal.


No. A hit means a name appeared in negative coverage. It may be about someone else, the customer may be a victim or a witness, and an allegation or a charge is not a conviction. Many matters are never prosecuted or end in dismissal, so the stage a matter reached is as important as the fact that it was reported.
